body:
Political activity in other Kathiawar states

Rajkot was an important centre of princely-state agitation, but political demands were not confined to it. Organisations and public movements also appeared in Bhavnagar, Gondal and Junagadh during the 1920s and 1930s. They raised concerns about civil liberties, public participation and the conduct of princely administrations.

The local conditions differed. A state with a limited representative institution did not face exactly the same political situation as one without such an institution. Similarly, an issue involving land revenue, a commercial monopoly or restrictions on political meetings could produce a movement with its own immediate demands.

What connected these organisations was the growing belief that the people of princely states had a right to participate in decisions affecting their lives. In Kathiawar, political workers such as Balwantrai Mehta contributed to the development of this wider regional movement.

From democratic demands to the question of accession

Before independence, a Praja Mandal or Praja Parishad primarily sought rights and accountable administration within a princely state. In 1947, a new constitutional question arose: what would happen to the princely states when British rule ended?

Under the arrangements accompanying independence, British paramountcy over the princely states lapsed. Rulers had to decide their states' future relationship with the new dominions. This created a major challenge for India's territorial unity.

Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, as Deputy Prime Minister and the minister responsible for states, played the leading political role in bringing princely states into the Indian Union. Negotiation and the signing of Instruments of Accession were central to this process.

Instrument of Accession

An Instrument of Accession was the legal document through which a princely ruler agreed that specified governmental subjects would come under the authority of the Dominion of India. Accession was an important constitutional step, but it was not necessarily identical to the later administrative merger of a state into a larger territorial unit.

Junagadh: a distinctive Gujarat case

Junagadh became a major accession dispute because its Nawab chose to accede to Pakistan in 1947, although Junagadh lay in Kathiawar and was surrounded by Indian territory except for its sea coast. The decision faced strong opposition among people who wanted the state to join India.

A provisional government, known as the Arzi Hukumat, emerged under Samaldas Gandhi. Its activity reflected opposition to the Nawab's decision. It should not be confused with an ordinary Praja Mandal: the immediate issue in 1947 was Junagadh's political future and accession.

After the Nawab left the state, the Government of India assumed Junagadh's administration on 9 November 1947 at the request of the Nawab's Council. A referendum held in February 1948 confirmed overwhelming support for accession to India.

Formation of the United State of Saurashtra

The numerous princely states of Kathiawar were consolidated into a larger administrative unit. The covenant establishing the United State of Saurashtra, also known initially as the United State of Kathiawar, was signed on 23 January 1948. Sardar Patel inaugurated the new state on 15 February 1948.

The integration of Junagadh followed a separate administrative timetable. Its administration was transferred from the Government of India to the Government of Saurashtra on 20 January 1949. This later transfer must not be mistaken for the inauguration of Saurashtra in February 1948.

The distinction between two historical processes

AspectPraja Mandal movementIntegration of princely states
Central questionWho should govern the people within a state?How should a princely state join and function within independent India?
Main demandCivil liberties and responsible governmentAccession and territorial-administrative consolidation
Principal periodEspecially the 1920s–1940sEspecially 1947–1949
Gujarat examplesKathiawar Rajkiya Parishad and Rajkot SatyagrahaJunagadh accession and the formation of Saurashtra

The processes were connected because popular demands for accountable government helped establish that the wishes of a state's inhabitants mattered. Nevertheless, the constitutional act of accession and the achievement of responsible government were not the same event.

Prelims focus

  • Princely-state political organisations also developed in Bhavnagar, Gondal and Junagadh.
  • British paramountcy over princely states lapsed in 1947.
  • Samaldas Gandhi was associated with Junagadh's Arzi Hukumat.
  • India assumed Junagadh's administration on 9 November 1947; a referendum followed in February 1948.
  • The Saurashtra covenant was signed on 23 January 1948, and the state was inaugurated on 15 February 1948.
  • Junagadh's administration transferred to Saurashtra on 20 January 1949.
  • Trap: Accession, the inauguration of Saurashtra and Junagadh's later administrative transfer were separate events.

[IGNOU, MHI-09, Unit 19, Political Democratisation in the Princely States, printed pp. 54–55, section 19.5, consulted 22 November 2026; NCERT, Politics in India Since Independence, Class 12, Chapter 1, Challenges of Nation Building, printed pp. 14–17; Government of India, Ministry of States, White Paper on Indian States, 1950, Part V, Formation of Unions: Saurashtra, paragraph 126, and Part XI, The Position of Junagadh State, paragraph 223; Ministry of External Affairs, Government of India, India-Pakistan documentary collection, correspondence concerning the Junagadh Provisional Government dated September 1947.]

pictures.alt: Two paths show Junagadh's accession and Saurashtra's formation, with inauguration on 15 February 1948 preceding Junagadh's transfer on 20 January 1949.
pictures.caption: The accession question and the administrative consolidation of Saurashtra proceeded through distinct stages.

title: Princely-State Movements Beyond Rajkot and the Integration of Saurashtra

body:
The first Gandhian ashram in India

After returning from South Africa in January 1915, Mahatma Gandhi sought to establish a community in which residents would practise truth, non-violence, self-discipline and service. He founded the Satyagraha Ashram at Kochrab, Ahmedabad, on 25 May 1915.

An ashram in this context was not simply a place of religious retreat. It was a residential community for practical training, collective discipline and social service. Its members were expected to connect personal conduct with public responsibilities.

Relocation to Sabarmati in 1917

The ashram was moved from Kochrab to a site on the banks of the Sabarmati River on 17 June 1917. The new location offered more scope for activities such as agriculture, animal husbandry, spinning, weaving and other forms of constructive work.

The institution became widely known as Sabarmati Ashram. Gandhi lived there during much of the period from 1917 to 1930, and it developed into a major centre of India's freedom struggle.

Kochrab, 1915: The first Gandhian ashram established in India. Sabarmati, 1917: The new site to which the ashram community moved. These dates describe establishment and relocation, not 2 unrelated movements.

Constructive work as preparation for political action

Gandhi believed that political freedom required changes in everyday social and economic life. Members of the ashram therefore undertook work intended to promote individual discipline, social equality and national self-reliance.

  • Spinning and khadi: Hand-spinning and hand-woven cloth encouraged self-reliance and gave practical expression to swadeshi, the preference for Indian-made goods and productive work.
  • Sanitation and manual labour: Shared physical work challenged the idea that particular tasks were beneath certain social groups.
  • Opposition to untouchability: The ashram's social principles challenged discrimination and linked national service with social reform.
  • Education and training: Community discipline helped prepare volunteers for service, organisation and non-violent resistance.
  • Truth and non-violence: Volunteers were expected to resist injustice without deliberately harming opponents.

These activities were connected with political mobilisation. A volunteer trained in self-discipline and collective work could participate more effectively in a satyagraha, help organise local campaigns and continue public service between major national movements.

Sabarmati Ashram and the Salt March

Sabarmati Ashram is closely associated with the Dandi Salt March of 1930. On 12 March 1930, Gandhi set out from Sabarmati with 78 selected companions. The march culminated at Dandi on the Gujarat coast, where Gandhi broke the salt law on 6 April 1930.

The march protested the British salt monopoly and tax. Salt was used by ordinary households across social and economic groups, making the issue understandable to a wide population. The journey also showed how a centre of constructive training could become the starting point of a major mass political movement.

Ashram and political organisation are different institutions

The ashram trained residents and volunteers and supported constructive activities. A Praja Mandal organised political demands within a princely state. A newspaper spread information and arguments. A national educational institution provided an alternative to colonial schooling. These different institutions supported public mobilisation, but their functions should not be confused.

Prelims focus

  • Kochrab Satyagraha Ashram was established at Ahmedabad on 25 May 1915.
  • The ashram shifted to Sabarmati on 17 June 1917.
  • Sabarmati Ashram became a major centre for constructive work and non-violent mobilisation.
  • Gandhi began the Dandi March from Sabarmati on 12 March 1930.
  • Gandhi broke the salt law at Dandi on 6 April 1930.
  • Trap: Kochrab and Sabarmati should not be treated as unrelated ashram movements.

[Sabarmati Ashram Preservation and Memorial Trust, History of Gandhi Ashram, sections on Kochrab and relocation to Sabarmati, consulted 22 November 2026; Gandhi Heritage Portal, Gandhi Heritage Sites, Kochrab Ashram and Sabarmati Ashram, consulted 22 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts – III, Class 8, Chapter 9, The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed pp. 115–118; Government of India, Rajghat Samadhi Committee, Life Events of Mahatma Gandhi, entries for March and April 1930, consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Residents spin yarn, weave cotton and share communal work in a simple Sabarmati Ashram courtyard around 1920.
pictures.caption: Spinning and cooperative work formed part of the everyday discipline of Sabarmati Ashram.

pictures.alt: Kochrab’s relocation to Sabarmati connects constructive work, volunteer preparation and the Dandi March, ending with the salt law broken.
pictures.caption: Sabarmati connected everyday constructive work with organised non-violent resistance.

title: Kochrab and Sabarmati Ashrams: Gandhi's Centres of Constructive Work and Mobilisation

body:
Why national educational institutions were established

Education became an important part of India's freedom movement because schools and colleges could shape public values, language use and future political leadership. During the Non-Cooperation Movement of 1920–1922, nationalists encouraged students and teachers to leave government-controlled educational institutions and support alternative systems of education.

The objective was not simply to change the language of teaching. Nationalist educators sought institutions that could develop independent thinking, public service, self-reliance and an understanding of India's social conditions.

Gujarat Vidyapith: foundation and purpose

Mahatma Gandhi founded Gujarat Vidyapith at Ahmedabad on 18 October 1920. It began as a national educational institution in the setting of the Non-Cooperation Movement. Gandhi remained its lifelong Kulpati, or Chancellor.

The institution aimed to educate students for national reconstruction. It connected intellectual learning with character formation, productive work and service to society. The use of Indian languages and attention to rural life formed part of this educational approach.

The establishment of Gujarat Vidyapith gave practical meaning to the boycott of colonial educational institutions. Students who rejected government-supported schooling needed a credible alternative if the movement was to continue beyond a symbolic protest.

Gujarat Vidyapith: Founded by Mahatma Gandhi on 18 October 1920 at Ahmedabad as a nationalist educational institution during the Non-Cooperation Movement.

Gujarat Mahavidyalaya and other national schools

Gujarat Mahavidyalaya was established in Ahmedabad on 15 November 1920 as an institution for higher learning associated with the national education initiative. It should be distinguished from Gujarat Vidyapith as the broader national educational institution.

In the princely state of Rajkot, Rashtriya Shala began on 2 February 1921 as a national school. It provided education in the spirit of the Non-Cooperation Movement and became associated with Gandhian constructive activities. The school later occupied premises supported by Rajkot's ruler, Lakhajiraj.

Rashtriya Shala also acquired political significance during the Rajkot Satyagraha of 1939, when Gandhi stayed there and undertook his fast in connection with the dispute over constitutional reform.

How national education supported mobilisation

National educational institutions helped sustain the freedom movement in several ways:

  • They provided alternative learning opportunities for students participating in the boycott of colonial education.
  • They encouraged familiarity with Indian languages and national political ideas.
  • They connected education with spinning, crafts, sanitation and community service.
  • They helped prepare students and teachers for voluntary public work.
  • They offered meeting places and networks through which political and social activities could continue.

Education was therefore part of the larger movement for swaraj, or self-government. However, Gujarat Vidyapith was an educational institution, not a Praja Mandal or a political party.

Prelims focus

  • Gujarat Vidyapith was founded by Mahatma Gandhi on 18 October 1920 at Ahmedabad.
  • It emerged during the Non-Cooperation Movement as a nationalist educational alternative.
  • Gandhi was its lifelong Chancellor.
  • Gujarat Mahavidyalaya was established on 15 November 1920.
  • Rashtriya Shala began at Rajkot on 2 February 1921.
  • Rashtriya Shala was connected with Gandhi's Rajkot fast in March 1939.
  • Trap: Gujarat Vidyapith, Gujarat Mahavidyalaya and Rajkot Rashtriya Shala were related to national education but were not the same institution.

[Gujarat Vidyapith, official Legacy and Objectives and organisational history, consulted 22 November 2026; Gujarat Vidyapith, Manual 1, Section 4(1)(b)(i), Particulars of Organisation, Functions and Duties; Gandhi Heritage Portal, Chronology of Mahatma Gandhi, entry for 18 October 1920, consulted 22 November 2026; The Indian Express, historical accounts of Rajkot's Rashtriya Shala published in 2019 and 2024, consulted 22 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts – III, Class 8, Chapter 9, section on the Non-Cooperation Movement, printed pp. 117–118.]

pictures.alt: Education boycott connected three distinct nationalist institutions with learning that prepared volunteers for public service and constructive work.
pictures.caption: National education connected institutional learning with public service and constructive work.

title: Gujarat Vidyapith, Rashtriya Shala and the National Education Movement
